extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, mathematics educators, and philosophers of mathematical practice
extracted.subtask_description: A rubric for judging the quality and explanatory power of mathematical proofs, framed around the reader's demonstrable abilities to reconstruct, adapt, and apply the argument rather than mere formal correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding as a cluster of abilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Understanding a proof is not a single mental state but a set of practical capacities a reader can exhibit; these capacities serve as the basis for judging understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the presence or absence of these abilities in readers as the primary criterion for whether a proof is 'understood' — this reframes understanding as observable skills rather than an internal label.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spell out implicit details
rubrics_metrics.description: The reader can reconstruct steps the author left implicit (the standard 'exercise' steps).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good exposition leaves routine details implicit but such that a competent reader can reliably fill them in; failing to make even the genuinely routine steps fillable is an exposition flaw. Example anti-pattern: skipping many small inferences that trained readers cannot easily reconstruct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify the main idea
rubrics_metrics.description: The reader can name the one or two key insights of the proof, distinguishing them from setup and bookkeeping.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a reader can summarize the core idea succinctly (e.g., in one sentence). Exposition should highlight or make accessible the central conceptual move rather than bury it in technicalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Locate the difficulty
rubrics_metrics.description: The reader can point to the steps that bear the real conceptual load — where the argument is genuinely hard or subtle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good proofs make it clear which maneuvers are pivotal; exposition failures often obscure which arguments are trivial bookkeeping versus which require new ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate next steps
rubrics_metrics.description: From a partial reading, the reader can predict where the proof is going and what the next steps will be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This ability indicates that the exposition has made the strategy visible; inability to anticipate often signals a lack of communicated strategy or conceptual framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize the role of each lemma
rubrics_metrics.description: The reader can explain why each lemma is needed and what would fail without it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A well-structured proof ties lemmas to the overall plan; gratuitous lemmas or opaque auxiliary results reduce understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modify the proof
rubrics_metrics.description: The reader can adapt the argument to slightly different hypotheses or to prove strengthened/variant conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capacity to modify indicates deeper mastery of the method; exposition should surface the assumptions and flexible points of the argument so readers can generalize or vary it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translate between presentations
rubrics_metrics.description: The reader can re-express the same proof in different notation, levels of formality, or stylistic registers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good exposition supports multiple representations (formal vs informal, diagrammatic vs symbolic); this helps learners with different cognitive styles and reveals the invariants of the argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize equivalent proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: The reader can see when two superficially different arguments are 'the same proof' (share core idea/structure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This ability shows that the reader grasps the underlying conceptual structure beyond surface details; exposition should make the structural skeleton visible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare to alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: The reader can articulate how this proof differs from or improves upon known alternative proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good exposition situates the proof historically or methodologically, noting trade-offs (e.g., simplicity vs generality) and when each approach is preferable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply the technique to new problems
rubrics_metrics.description: The reader can use the method or technique of the proof to tackle new, related problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A proof that yields transferable techniques demonstrates real explanatory power; exposition should abstract and highlight the method so it can be reused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justify the choice of definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: The reader can explain why the concepts/definitions used in the proof are appropriate and how they 'cut the problem at its joints.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exposition should motivate definitions by showing how they streamline arguments or reveal structure; arbitrary-seeming definitions without justification hinder understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exposition enables acquisition of abilities
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof's exposition is judged by how well it enables readers to acquire the listed abilities (reconstruction, identification, modification, application, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a meta-criterion: beyond formal correctness, evaluate whether the text supports learning and demonstration of the practical capacities that constitute understanding. Empirical evidence (e.g., whether readers can perform these tasks) is relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calibration of implicitness (operate in the gap)
rubrics_metrics.description: Good exposition leaves implicit those things a trained reader can reliably fill in and makes explicit what a competent reader cannot; exposition should operate 'in the gap' between full formal detail and too much omission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mismatches in calibration are exposition failures — either overspecifying trivial steps (burdensome formal detail) or omitting subtle steps (leaving readers unable to reconstruct). The ideal balance depends on the intended audience's competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding is not reducible to formal correctness
rubrics_metrics.description: A fully formal, machine-checked derivation can be logically perfect yet typically fail to yield human understanding; logical validity is necessary but not sufficient for explanatory quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating proof quality, include explanatory and pedagogical dimensions in addition to formal correctness. Computer-verified proofs are evidence that correctness ≠ understanding; thus rubrics must include human-centered abilities.
